analysis.one_liner: Guarantees whistleblowers at least 10% of penalties collected when they expose money laundering and financial crimes.
analysis.headline: The bill passed a House committee unanimously but never received a vote by the full House or Senate before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have strengthened the government's program that pays insiders for exposing financial crimes like money laundering. It guarantees a whistleblower at least 10% of any penalty the government collects based on their tip (up to 30%), creates a dedicated Financial Integrity Fund paid for by those penalties rather than taxpayer appropriations, and covers additional laws including sanctions statutes. It passed a House committee in June 2022 but was never scheduled for a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.who_benefits: Ordinary people benefit indirectly: stronger financial incentives and guaranteed minimum payouts make it more likely that bank employees and other insiders report money laundering, sanctions evasion, and other financial crimes, since awards come from the penalties collected, not from taxpayers' pockets. Whistleblowers themselves are direct beneficiaries, gaining a guaranteed minimum of 10% and up to 30% of collected sanctions, plus a dedicated fund that insulates their awards.

how_it_helps.text: Raises the guaranteed whistleblower award to at least 10% of collected sanctions and caps it at 30%, making it financially safer for insiders to report banks and other institutions engaged in money laundering or sanctions evasion [S3] [S4].
Creates a dedicated, self-funding Financial Integrity Fund so awards are paid out of collected penalties and its investment income, rather than depending on annual appropriations [S4].
Extends covered awards to cases involving sanctions laws, the Trading With the Enemy Act, and drug-kingpin statutes, broadening the conduct insiders can be paid to report [S2] [S3] [S4].

analysis.who_pays: Financial institutions that violate money-laundering and sanctions laws bear the cost, since whistleblower tips funded by collected sanctions make detection more likely. General Treasury revenue loses a small share of collected sanctions to fund the award pool.

drawbacks.text: The Financial Integrity Fund diverts a share of collected monetary sanctions away from the Treasury's general revenues and victim funds (the bill expressly carves out the State Sponsored Terrorism and Crime Victims Funds, but the general flow of sanctions into a dedicated whistleblower pot reduces money available for other purposes) — a cost an honest supporter would acknowledge [S4].

The bill strengthens incentives for a single existing award program under the Treasury Secretary; it does not expand anti-retaliation protections or reach other whistleblower programs, so its practical impact is limited to the narrow universe of money-laundering and sanctions cases [S2] [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The main benefit—raising the guaranteed floor for financial-crime whistleblowers from an optional award to a minimum of 10% of collections—is real but modest, and the cost is essentially zero because awards come from the sanctions the wrongdoing generates rather than from taxpayers. The bill's scope is narrow: it strengthens one existing award program rather than expanding whistleblower protection against retaliation. Its main weakness is political, not design: it never got a floor vote in either chamber, so it delivered nothing.

outcome.mechanism: The House Financial Services Committee approved it and placed it on the House calendar, but no vote was ever scheduled in the House or Senate before the Congress ended, so it died there.

narrative.text: Rep. Alma Adams introduced the bill in March 2022 with Rep. Anthony Gonzalez as original cosponsor [S1] [S6] [S5].
The House Financial Services Committee held a markup on June 22, 2022, and ordered the bill reported as amended by voice vote [S6].
The committee formally reported the amended bill on July 20, 2022, and it was placed on the Union Calendar (Calendar No. 329), the House's list of bills awaiting floor action [S1] [S6].
No further action was taken; the bill never received a House floor vote and was never taken up by the Senate before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023 [S6].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Financial institutions facing whistleblower risk are better off, since nothing changed; no one else gained.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Financial institutions; the bill died untouched

sides.party_line_note: The bill moved through committee with bipartisan support (reported by voice vote with a Republican cosponsor), and no party bloc opposed it on the record; it simply was never scheduled for a floor vote.

industries.industry: Banks, money transmitters, and other financial institutions
industries.note: The bill raises guaranteed payouts to insiders who report money laundering, sanctions evasion, and related financial crimes, and extends covered awards to sanctions and drug-kingpin cases. It relies on collected sanctions to fund awards, so enforcement actions against financial institutions could produce larger whistleblower payouts, increasing the risk an employee speaks up rather than stay quiet.

A share of monetary sanctions that would otherwise flow to general Treasury revenue is instead dedicated to the whistleblower fund, though the bill keeps victim funds untouched. The cost is small relative to the deterrence benefit for ordinary people.
